Hypertension

A short blue-light exposure lowered systolic pressure in a small healthy-volunteer crossover study. A randomized post-mastectomy study found no between-group difference in systolic or diastolic pressure, while several rat models reported lower pressure. Sustained benefit in people with diagnosed hypertension has not been established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A short blue-light exposure lowered systolic pressure in a small healthy-volunteer crossover study. A randomized post-mastectomy study found no between-group difference in systolic or diastolic pressure, while several rat models reported lower pressure. Sustained benefit in people with diagnosed hypertension has not been established.

Summary of the Evidence

Fourteen publications are classified under the hypertension indication: five human reports, seven rat experiments, one systematic review with meta-analysis, and one clinical-trial protocol. The human reports include two randomized studies and three non-randomized studies. The review screened 197 records and included four randomized trials and five experimental studies; its included studies overlap the wider research literature and should not be added as nine new articles to the category count. Ocular-hypertension records are outside this indication summary.

Human and clinical evidence

The randomized clinical trial most directly examining people with hypertension enrolled 27 women treated after mastectomy and taking hormone blockers. Intravascular laser irradiation was directed near the carotid artery. Systolic and diastolic pressure did not differ significantly between groups, although heart rate fell in the treatment group (Pacheco et al. 2024).

A randomized crossover experiment in 14 healthy adults found that whole-body visible blue-light exposure lowered systolic pressure and improved arterial-stiffness and endothelial measures. This is evidence of a short-term physiological response in healthy volunteers, not a treatment trial for diagnosed hypertension (Stern et al. 2018). Other small or non-randomized reports examined blood pressure during musculoskeletal treatment or in people with hyperuricemia, so they do not isolate PBM as a hypertension therapy. The 2025 systematic review reported possible reductions in systolic pressure, diastolic pressure, and heart rate, but rated certainty very low because of bias and limitations in the primary studies (Espósito et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

Seven rat publications used models including spontaneous, renovascular, diet-associated, or hormone-related hypertension. Several reported lower blood pressure after red-light treatment, though not all animals responded equally. A dose-comparison experiment found a larger response at an intermediate energy and no hypotensive response at the highest tested exposure. A longer study in high-fat-diet rats reported prevention of a blood-pressure rise alongside changes in nitric oxide and endothelial function (Oishi et al. 2024).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One rat publication also included laboratory work on vasodilation and nitric-oxide-related mechanisms. This is part of that animal publication, not a separate hypertension trial.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human protocols are not interchangeable. The post-mastectomy study used 660-nm visible red light near the carotid artery for 15 minutes across 16 sessions over four weeks. The paper and database differ on the reported energy per session, so that value is omitted here. The healthy-volunteer experiment used 450-nm visible blue light over the body for 30 minutes. Rat studies most often used 660-nm red light, with some 780- or 830-nm near-infrared light. No clinical head-to-head or dose-finding trial has established which wavelength, site, or schedule is best.

Interpretation

Whole-body blue visible light lowered systolic pressure and improved arterial-stiffness and endothelial measures in a small crossover study of healthy adults. In contrast, a randomized post-mastectomy study found no significant between-group difference in systolic or diastolic pressure. Several rat hypertension models reported lower pressure. The human physiological and animal findings are favorable in selected settings, but sustained blood-pressure control in diagnosed hypertension has not been demonstrated.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for sustained blood-pressure control in diagnosed hypertension Low for short-term blood-pressure changes in selected light-exposure settings
Publications and records14 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A short blue-light crossover in healthy adults lowered systolic pressure, and several rat models also reported reductions. In contrast, a randomized post-mastectomy study found no between-group difference in systolic or diastolic pressure, and sustained benefit in diagnosed hypertension remains unproven. Larger sham-controlled studies in hypertensive patients with longer follow-up would be needed to support a stronger clinical rating.
